items.title: A mole of marshmallows would cover the USA 600 miles deep
items.claim: 6.022 times 10 to the 23 is just a number until you try to picture it. Avogadro's number of marshmallows would bury the entire surface of the United States to a depth of 600 miles.
items.prompt: Roughly how many moles of water molecules are in a single drop (about 0.05 mL)?

options.text: About 0.003 moles, which is roughly 1.7 times 10 to the 21 molecules
Around 6 times 10 to the 23 — one drop is one mole
About 0.05 moles, the same as the volume in millilitres

items.reveal_title: Even a microscopic drop contains stupefying numbers of molecules
items.reveal:
0.05 mL of water has a mass of 0.05 g. Water is 18 g per mole, so 0.05 / 18 equals about 0.0028 mol. Multiply by Avogadro's number and you get roughly 1.7 times 10 to the 21 molecules.

If you counted those molecules at one per second, it would take about 50 trillion years — over 3000 times the age of the universe. Chemistry is the study of mind-bending counts of incredibly tiny things.
items.why: The mole is treated as a unit conversion when it should be treated as a stark statement about scale.

items.title: Most of the universe is in a state of matter not taught at GCSE
items.claim: Solid, liquid, gas. The three states of matter on the syllabus. But more than 99 percent of the visible matter in the universe is in a fourth state: plasma. Stars are plasma. Lightning is plasma. The Sun is a giant ball of plasma.
items.prompt: What makes plasma different from a gas?

options.text: Plasma is hotter than a gas
In a plasma the atoms have been ionised — electrons and nuclei move independently — so the substance responds to electric and magnetic fields, conducts electricity, and emits its own light
Plasma is denser than a gas
Plasma is liquid that has been heated

items.reveal_title: Plasma is everywhere — except down here
items.reveal:
Heat any gas enough and electrons are stripped from nuclei. The collection of free electrons and ions is a plasma. Stars, ionised interstellar medium, neon signs, fluorescent lamps, lightning bolts, and the auroras are all plasmas.

Plasmas conduct electricity (free charges) and respond strongly to magnetic fields (charged-particle motion produces magnetic fields and vice versa). The whole of magnetohydrodynamics deals with plasma behaviour.

Fusion energy research (ITER, JET) depends on confining a hot hydrogen plasma at over 100 million K using magnetic fields. The plasma can't touch any solid wall — the wall would vaporise long before the plasma cooled.
items.why: The 'three states' taught at GCSE describe Earth-surface chemistry. Cosmically, plasma is the default.

items.title: Gases mix even when there is nothing to gain energetically
items.claim: Open a bottle of perfume. It spreads through the room. The process releases essentially zero heat — there is no chemistry. Yet it is utterly spontaneous and would NEVER spontaneously reverse.
items.prompt: What drives mixing if there's no enthalpy change?

options.text: Entropy of mixing — there are vastly more microstates where perfume molecules are spread throughout the room than concentrated in the bottle; the system follows the overwhelming statistical probability

items.reveal:
For two ideal gases mixing at constant T and P, delta H is zero. But delta S equals -nR(x1 ln x1 + x2 ln x2), which is always positive for mixing. Gibbs free energy delta G = delta H - T delta S is therefore negative — mixing is spontaneous.

The perfume could in principle un-mix back into the bottle. The probability of all the molecules randomly returning is roughly 1 in 10 to the 10 to the 23 — for practical purposes, zero.

This is the statistical foundation of the second law: irreversibility is a matter of counting configurations, not of broken time symmetry.
items.why: Spontaneity is taught as 'releases energy'. Entropy alone, with no enthalpy change at all, can drive a process firmly.
